questions.explanation: Only positive steps are used, so the limit is one-sided along the ray. A two-sided limit would ask the slice to be differentiable at 0, which is stronger and can fail at a corner. Adding partial derivatives is a different object, and it needs those partials to exist. The length of \(d\) does not involve \(f\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
options: the limit of \([f(x + t d) - f(x)] / t\) as \(t\) decreases to 0
the two-sided limit of that same quotient as \(t\) tends to 0
the sum of the partial derivatives at \(x\)
the length of the direction \(d\)

questions.explanation: Along \(x = 3 + t\), \(y = 1\), the difference quotient is \(6 + t\), and the limit is 6. The same value is \(2 \cdot 3 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot 0\). The partial derivative in \(y\) is 4, and that is the derivative in the direction \((0, 1)\), not in \((1, 0)\). The function value \(9 + 4 = 13\) is not a slope.

questions.prompt: When \(c > 0\) and both derivatives exist, \(f'(x; c d)\) equals
questions.explanation: A positive scale runs along the same ray at a different speed, and the difference quotient picks up that factor. Leaving the factor out treats every positive scale as the same direction vector. Dividing by \(c\) runs the scaling backwards. Adding \(c\) is not how a slope transforms.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order used to compute \(f'(x; d)\) from the definition.
questions.explanation: The definition builds one difference quotient and then takes a one-sided limit. The point on the ray has to come first, because the numerator uses it. Division by t comes after the numerator exists. The limit is last. Dividing before subtracting, or sending t to 0 through negative values, computes a different limit.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
steps: Form the point x + t d with t positive.
Subtract f(x) from the value at that point.
Take the limit as t decreases to 0.

questions.explanation: The slice is \(y = 1 + t\) with \(x\) fixed at 3. Then \(f = 9 + 4 + 4t\), so the quotient is 4. The partial derivative in \(x\) at this point is \(2 \cdot 3 = 6\), which belongs to the direction \((1, 0)\). The product \(4 \cdot 1 = 4\) happens to match because the direction's second coordinate is 1; the function value 13 is not the slope.

questions.explanation: The formula \(2 x\, d_1 + 4 d_2\) gives \(2 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot (-1) = 8\). On the slice, \(f(3 + 2t, 1 - t) = 13 + 8t + 4t^2\), so the quotient tends to 8. Using only the first partial gives 6. Using only the second gives 4. The squared length of the direction is \(4 + 1 = 5\), which is not the slope.

questions.prompt: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be real. At \((1, 0)\), the directional derivative of \(a x^2 + b y\) in the direction \((1, 1)\) is an expression in the names a and b. Write that expression.
questions.explanation:
The partial derivative in \(x\) is \(2 a x\), which equals \(2a\) at \(x = 1\). The partial derivative in \(y\) is \(b\). The direction \((1, 1)\) adds them, so the derivative is \(2a + b\).
• \(2a\) drops the second coordinate of the direction.
• \(a + b\) differentiates \(a x^2\) as if it were \(a x\).
• \(ab\) multiplies the two coefficients. The direction asks for a sum.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.explanation: \(2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 + 4 \cdot 1 = 16\). The function value at \((2, 5)\) is \(4 + 20 = 24\), which is not a slope. The sum of the direction coordinates is 4. The partial derivative in \(x\) alone is 4 at this point, and that would be the answer only for the direction \((1, 0)\).

questions.prompt: For the slice \(g(t) = f(x + t d)\), the directional derivative equals
questions.explanation: Positive \(t\) is the right-hand side of the slice, so the directional derivative is \(g'(0+)\). The two-sided derivative can fail while the right-hand derivative exists. One secant, from \(-1\) to \(1\), is a difference quotient at a fixed step, not the limit. The value \(g(0)\) is \(f(x)\), not a slope.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
options: the two-sided derivative \(g'(0)\), even when that limit fails
the slope of the secant from \(t = -1\) to \(t = 1\)
the right-hand derivative of \(g\) at 0
the value \(g(0)\)

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for this one-sided directional derivative?
questions.explanation: The definition is that one-sided limit, and a positive rescaling multiplies the quotient by the same positive factor. A gradient is a later, stronger object: the directional derivative along one ray can exist with no gradient. At a corner the two opposite rays can both give a positive slope, so the map \(d \mapsto f'(x; d)\) need not be linear. The inner product with a gradient is the case where linearity does hold.

options: It is a limit of difference quotients as the step decreases to 0.
For \(c > 0\), the derivative in the direction \(c d\) is \(c\) times the derivative in the direction \(d\), when both exist.
It exists only after a gradient has been shown to exist.
It is always linear in the direction, including at a corner of the slice.

questions.prompt: What is the directional derivative of \(f(x) = \lvert x \rvert\) at \(0\) in the direction \(3\)?
questions.explanation: For \(t > 0\), \([\lvert 3t \rvert - 0] / t = 3\). The limit is 3. The direction \(-3\) gives \([\lvert -3t \rvert] / t = 3\) as well, so the two rays do not produce opposite signs. The two-sided derivative of \(\lvert x \rvert\) at 0 does not exist; that is a different limit. Dividing the result by 3 produces the derivative in the unit direction, not in the direction 3.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: At a corner of \(\lvert x \rvert\), the one-sided directional derivatives
questions.explanation: Leaving 0 in either direction increases \(\lvert x \rvert\), so both one-sided derivatives are positive. They exist. They are not zero, and they are not negative. What fails is the two-sided derivative on the line, and with it any claim that the directional derivative is linear in \(d\). A later differentiability test is what rules this corner out.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
options: fail to exist in every direction
are negative in every direction
are zero in every direction
can be positive both along \(d\) and along \(-d\)
